title: Two friends, five feet and six feet: who is who?
description: A busy railway platform shows that people differ in height. Two outline figures, one five feet and one six feet tall, wait for a guess that nobody can be sure about.
teaching_notes: One idea: a sensible guess about one person comes from the pattern seen in many people, and it can still be wrong. Watch for children who say the guess must be certain before they will make it.

source: Guessing from experience: two friends of different heights
video_script.why: The child has seen many people but has never named the habit of guessing about one person from what is common in a group.
video_script.substitution: A guess about one person rests on the pattern seen in many people.
video_script.anchor: Two childhood friends of the teacher: one is five feet tall, the other is six feet tall
maths_rules: one friend is 5 feet tall and the other is 6 feet tall, as in the book
no rule fixes a person's height; the guess rests on what is common in many people
the guess can be wrong for one person and still be a sensible guess
video_script.design: Opener only: a real crowd, then two outline figures with their heights, then the open question. No answer is given and no term is named.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Look at the people on this busy railway platform.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Some are tall, some are short, and most are somewhere in between.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Your teacher is meeting two childhood friends this evening.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>One friend is five feet tall.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>The other friend is six feet tall.

beats.on_screen: the two figures stay with their labels; a thought cloud fills with many small figures of different heights; the question line sits under them

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Nobody has told you whether each friend is a man or a woman.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Still, you have seen many people in your life.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Which friend is more likely to be the man, and what makes you think so?
